A chip in your document
Biometric passports and recent identity cards contain a contactless chip that follows the international ICAO 9303 standard.
ICAO: the International Civil Aviation Organization, which sets the rules for travel documents.
The chip holds a copy of the printed information and the photo, electronically signed by the country that issued the document.
A key to open the chip
Without a key, the chip refuses to answer. The key is printed on the document:
CAN: the 6-digit access number printed on the front of most recent identity cards.
MRZ: the lines of characters at the bottom of the passport photo page or on the back of the card, which give the document number, date of birth and expiry date.
All exchanges then go through an encrypted channel (PACE or BAC, the protocols defined by the standard): someone nearby who does not know this key cannot read them.
What Sceau checks
The issuing country’s signature (Passive Authentication), using the country certificates built into the app or that you have imported.
That the chip is not a copy (Chip Authentication or Active Authentication): it must prove it holds a secret key that it never reveals.
The result comes down to four verdicts:
Your data stays here
Everything happens on the phone: Sceau does not even have permission to access the internet.
Nothing is saved: the data read is erased as soon as you leave the result or the app goes to the background.
Screenshots are blocked throughout the app.
Understanding Sceau
Replay the introduction
What the chip contains
Back
The chip stores its information in files: data groups (DG1, DG2…) and a few technical files whose names start with EF. Here is what Sceau does with them.
Read and displayed
The MRZ data: document type, surname, given names, nationality, date of birth, sex, document number, issuing country and expiry date.
The holder’s photo.
If the country records it: an image of the holder’s handwritten signature.
If the country records it: additional personal details, such as place of birth or address.
If the country records it: details about the document, such as the issuing authority and date of issue, sometimes an image of the document.
Read for verification only
These files contain no personal data: they are used to communicate with the chip and to prove that the data is authentic.
The access protocols the chip accepts, such as PACE.
The list of data groups present.
The hash of each data group, signed by the issuing country.
The public key used for Chip Authentication.
The public key used for Active Authentication.
On some documents only (PACE-CAM): the chip’s key signed by the issuing country, which confirms that the chip authenticated itself while the channel was being opened.
Never read
Fingerprints.
The iris image.
On European documents, these two files are protected by an extra lock anyway, EAC (Extended Access Control), which only authorized authorities can open.
The other data groups (DG5, DG6, DG8 to DG10, DG13 and DG16: other portrait, reserved slot, document security features, country-specific data, persons to notify) are not read either.
What Sceau does not do
It does not save, send or log any data read: everything stays in the phone’s memory and is erased when you leave the result.
It allows neither screenshots nor a preview in recent apps.
It writes no data to the chip: it only reads it.
It reads nothing other than the files listed above: no other information on the chip, of any kind, is requested.
